nameStory: Hutchins' Pincushion gets its charming name from its growth habit – it forms neat, rounded cushions that look remarkably like old-fashioned pincushions used for sewing. The species honors Thomas Hutchins, an 18th-century naturalist and fur trader who explored the Arctic regions of North America and collected many plant specimens.
description: Hutchins' Pincushion is a small moss that forms dense, rounded cushions on tree bark, typically growing less than an inch tall. The tiny plants cluster together so tightly they create what looks like a soft, green pillow attached to branches and trunks. When dry, the moss appears grayish-green and somewhat shriveled, but after rain it transforms into a vibrant emerald cushion. Like other mosses, it reproduces by spores rather than flowers or seeds.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms distinctive rounded cushions or dome-shaped patches on tree bark, rarely more than 3/4 inch across and looking remarkably like tiny green pincushions

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves are lance-shaped and curl inward when dry, creating a twisted, crimped appearance that relaxes when wet

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and springy when moist, like a miniature sponge, but becomes crispy and brittle when completely dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shifts dramatically from dull grayish-green when dry to bright emerald green when wet, making it much more noticeable after rain

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on tree bark, particularly favoring the north sides of deciduous trees and avoiding rocks or soil

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces small, urn-shaped capsules on short stalks that emerge from the cushion center, visible mainly in late spring and early summer

habitat: Hutchins' Pincushion grows exclusively on the bark of trees, showing a preference for deciduous species like maples, birches, and oaks throughout New England's forests. It particularly favors the shaded, north-facing sides of tree trunks and larger branches where moisture lingers longer. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, often in mixed woodlands and forest edges where humidity stays relatively high.

seasonality.spring: Cushions become most vibrant and noticeable as frequent rains keep them hydrated and bright green. Sporophyte capsules begin developing and are most visible during this season.
seasonality.summer: May appear less prominent during dry spells when cushions shrink and turn grayish, but look for them after summer thunderstorms when they quickly plump up and turn emerald green.
seasonality.fall: Remains active and visible, often standing out more clearly against bare bark as leaves fall and expose more trunk surfaces to view.
seasonality.winter: Stays present year-round but appears dormant and grayish during dry, cold periods. Becomes temporarily vibrant during winter thaws and wet spells.

funFact: Hutchins' Pincushion can absorb up to 20 times its dry weight in water and completely transform from a shriveled, almost dead-looking gray patch to a plump, vibrant green cushion in less than 10 minutes after a rainstorm begins!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Crisped Pincushion moss, but Hutchins' forms tighter, more dome-shaped cushions while Crisped Pincushion tends to spread in looser, more irregular patches. Remember: Hutchins' = neat little domes, Crisped = messy sprawls.
compareHints: Hutchins' Pincushion forms the tightest, most perfectly dome-shaped cushions of all the Ulota species in New England, while Crisped Pincushion spreads more loosely and Club Pincushion tends to grow in more elongated patches. The cushion shape in Hutchins' is so distinctive that it's often described as the most 'pincushion-like' of all the pincushion mosses. When wet, Hutchins' maintains its compact dome shape better than its relatives, which tend to spread out more when hydrated.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives in the Ulota genus, crisped pincushion shows the most dramatic leaf curling when dry—much more pronounced than Hutchins' pincushion or club pincushion.
Compared to Crisped Pincushion (Ulota crispa), Curly Ulota has more uniformly curled leaves and tends to form denser cushions.
Among the pincushion mosses, Club Pincushion is distinguished by its very short sporophyte stalks compared to Crisped Pincushion's longer ones.
Compared to the more common crisped pincushion (Ulota crispa), Ulota intermedia forms smaller, more compact cushions and typically has shorter, less prominently curled leaves when dry.
